verses.text: That same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet, who was of Gibeon, spoke to me in Yahweh’s house, in the presence of the priests and of all the people, saying,
“Thus speaks Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, saying, ‘I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.
Within two full years will I bring again into this place all the vessels of Yahweh’s house, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place, and carried to Babylon.
I will bring again to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, with all the captives of Judah, who went to Babylon,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.’”
Then the prophet Jeremiah said to the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests, and in the presence of all the people who stood in Yahweh’s house,

even the prophet Jeremiah said, “Amen! May Yahweh do so. May Yahweh perform your words which you have prophesied, to bring again the vessels of Yahweh’s house, and all them of the captivity, from Babylon to this place.
Nevertheless listen now to this word that I speak in your ears, and in the ears of all the people:
The prophets who have been before me and before you of old prophesied against many countries, and against great kingdoms, of war, and of evil, and of pestilence.
The prophet who prophesies of peace, when the word of the prophet shall happen, then shall the prophet be known, that Yahweh has truly sent him.”
Then Hananiah the prophet took the bar from off the prophet Jeremiah’s neck, and broke it.

Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, “Yahweh says: ‘Even so I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon within two full years from off the neck of all the nations.’” Then the prophet Jeremiah went his way.
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah, after that Hananiah the prophet had broken the bar from off the neck of the prophet Jeremiah, saying,
“Go, and tell Hananiah, saying, ‘Yahweh says, “You have broken the bars of wood, but you have made in their place bars of iron.”

For Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel says, “I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and they will serve him. I have also given him the animals of the field.”’”
Then the prophet Jeremiah said to Hananiah the prophet, “Listen, Hananiah! Yahweh has not sent you, but you make this people trust in a lie.
Therefore Yahweh says, ‘Behold, I will send you away from off the surface of the earth. This year you will die, because you have spoken rebellion against Yahweh.’”
So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.

footnotes.content: Here in the temple, before priests and all the people, a false prophet named Hananiah stood and contradicted Jeremiah's hard word about captivity. Sometimes the greatest test of faith isn't the enemy's shout, but a brother's soothing lie spoken in God's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hananiah's first words sound so assured—'I have broken the yoke.' But an assertion of freedom God hasn't pronounced is just wishful speech wrapped in His name. How gently the Lord must grieve when we comfort ourselves with what we want to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Within two full years"—Hananiah gives a date, makes it specific. False prophets often do; true prophets speak with God's uncertain courage. The promise itself was beautiful: the vessels of the temple returned, the exile reversed. But a beautiful lie is still a lie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king Jeconiah would return, the captives restored—words that comforted many ears. Yet God had spoken a harder truth through Jeremiah. When comfort contradicts God's revealed word, it feeds our rebellion, not our faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah responds in the same setting, before the same crowd. He doesn't dismiss Hananiah with scorn, but addresses him as 'prophet,' acknowledging what everyone sees—a man who speaks with authority. Truth can afford to listen; it doesn't need to shout first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah says 'Amen'—he too wishes it were true. He speaks for return, restoration, hope; his heart bends the same way as the crowd's. But wishing doesn't make it so, and the prophet's burden is to tell us what is, not what we'd prefer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah asks for ears to listen, not just emotions to stir. He moves toward his hard distinction: one prophet soothes, one warns. The crowd must decide whom to trust with their souls—and the only way is to test their words against God's pattern.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah reaches into history: the real prophets before him—Isaiah, Hosea, Amos—spoke judgment against nations and kings, not endless assurance. War, evil, pestilence—they named the hard reality. A prophet who only soothes breaks faith with the prophetic line.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's the test: when it happens, we'll know. Jeremiah gives both prophets over to time and God's judgment. The man who speaks for peace will be proven true only if his words come to pass. This is humility and confidence at once—truth doesn't hide from the future.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wooden yoke Jeremiah wore—a sign of Babylon's iron grip—Hananiah seized and broke it. A symbolic gesture meant to seal his prophecy, to make his words visible. Signs and wonders move the crowd faster than argument ever could.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hananiah speaks again, his confidence heightened by the broken yoke in his hands. The crowd sees power. Jeremiah simply walks away—not in anger, but in obedience. He's said his piece, shown the test, and now steps aside to let God judge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After Hananiah's grand gesture, God's word comes to Jeremiah. Not in the crowd, not in the moment—but afterward, in the quiet. Sometimes we must wait for God's word to come when the noise of the false prophet has faded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'You have broken the bars of wood, but you have made in their place bars of iron.' God's word turns Hananiah's symbol against him—his own act becomes a sign of the opposite truth. In breaking what he broke, he's only made the bondage heavier.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks plainly: the yoke of Babylon is not wood to snap, but iron on the nations' necks. Nebuchadnezzar's reign will not be broken in two years; it will persist because God has put it there. The exile is real, certain, and the only path through it is obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah confronts Hananiah again, this time with the weight of God's word behind him. 'Yahweh has not sent you.' It's the most dangerous accusation a true prophet can make—and it cuts to the heart. Hananiah didn't lie by accident; he led people to trust in false security.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God judges Hananiah: he will die this year, in the seventh month, for speaking rebellion against the Lord. It's a swift and terrible consequence—not delayed, not ambiguous, but certain. The false prophet who lifted hearts on a lie finds his own life cut short.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: And it came to pass: Hananiah died that same year. Looking back from a longer road, readers today hear an echo in this—how often the Lord vindicates His true prophets not by might or signs, but by the simple fact that His word alone comes to pass. We live in an age of many voices; the test remains unchanged.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
